title: Widest Step Around the Ring
statement:
You get an array nums arranged in a ring: after the last element comes the first one again. Two elements are neighbours if they sit next to each other in this ring, so the last and the first element are neighbours too.

Return the largest absolute difference between any two neighbours.

examples.why: The steps are |3 − 8| = 5, |8 − 6| = 2 and, around the ring, |6 − 3| = 3.
Inside the array the widest step is 11, but the wrap-around step from 20 back to 1 is 19.
With two elements both steps are the same pair.

hints: Each element has a right-hand neighbour. Which index is that for the last element?
The right neighbour of index i is (i + 1) % n.
Loop i from 0 to n − 1 and take the maximum of |nums[i] − nums[(i + 1) % n]|.

explain.intuition: A ring of n elements has exactly n neighbouring pairs: the n − 1 pairs inside the array plus one pair that wraps from the end back to the start. Modulo arithmetic turns that wrap into a normal index, the same trick used for a carousel that loops from the last slide back to the first.
steps: For each i from 0 to n − 1, let j = (i + 1) % n.
pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around pair, as in [1, 4, 9, 20].
Returning max − min of the whole array. The largest and smallest values need not be neighbours: in [1, 5, 9, 5] every step is 4, not 8.
Overflow in typed languages: the difference can reach 2·10<sup>9</sup>, beyond a 32-bit int.

solutions.title: Modulo neighbour
solutions.idea: Every index looks at (i + 1) % n, which covers the wrap-around pair automatically.

solutions.title: Linear scan plus the wrap pair
solutions.idea: Scan the n − 1 inner pairs, then start from the last-to-first pair as the initial best.

followups: You may rotate the ring freely but not reorder it. Does that change the answer? Why not?
You may reorder the elements however you like. Arrange them to make the widest step as small as possible.
